section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Normal Distribution
section_1.content: Briefly define the 'Bell Curve' (Normal Distribution). Explain that it is defined by its mean and standard deviation, and is symmetrical.
section_1.example: Visual: An animation of a perfectly symmetrical bell-shaped curve flattening and sharpening based on changing standard deviation parameters.

section_2.title: The Problem: Randomness in the Wild
section_2.content: Introduce the concept that most real-world data is NOT normally distributed (e.g., uniform, skewed, or discrete distributions). We explain the need to predict behavior when sampling.
section_2.example: Visual: Showing a 'Dice Roll' distribution. One die shows a flat, uniform distribution. Ask: 'What happens if we roll 50 dice at once?'

section_3.title: The Core Concept: Sampling Distributions
section_3.content: Define the Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean. Explain that even if the population is non-normal, the average of those samples will start to behave differently.
section_3.example: Visual: Three distinct colored buckets (Uniform, Skewed, Binomial). As samples are pulled and averaged, the resulting plot lines start to morph into a singular Bell Curve.

section_4.title: The Central Limit Theorem Defined
section_4.content: State the theorem: As sample size (n) increases, the distribution of sample means approaches a Normal Distribution, regardless of the original population's shape.
section_4.example: Visual: A 'Race to Normality' animation. A highly skewed distribution of 'Bird Migration Distances' transforms into a perfect Bell Curve as 'n' increases from 2 to 30.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: The Law of Averages
section_5.content: Explain why this matters: It allows us to perform hypothesis testing and build confidence intervals even without knowing the underlying population distribution.
section_5.example: Visual: A Quality Control engineer monitoring a factory robot. Despite the machine having irregular performance spikes, the 'hourly average' output creates a predictable Bell Curve, allowing the engineer to spot outliers.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=20, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
